case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana’s COVID-era Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity—requiring gross negligence or willful misconduct—may be applied in state court to bar or heighten the elements of federal disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act arising from a healthcare provider’s denial of treatment during the declared public health emergency.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) civil-liability immunity provisions (as applied during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency), in interaction with Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189, and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (RA), 29 U.S.C. § 794 (including federal remedial limitations recognized by Supreme Court precedent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Louisiana courts wrongly used LHEPA to effectively displace or rewrite federal civil-rights causes of action by importing a heightened state-law fault standard (gross negligence/willful misconduct) into ADA Title III and RA § 504 claims. In petitioner’s view, this converts federal antidiscrimination claims into something akin to state tort claims, undermines uniform nationwide enforcement of federal disability rights, and is preempted because a state immunity statute cannot narrow federally created rights and remedies. Petitioner also contends it is ‘absurd’ to apply emergency healthcare immunity to a denial of aquatic therapy unrelated to COVID-19 treatment, and that the Louisiana Supreme Court erred by denying review on state-immunity grounds without addressing the federal merits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the petition rests on a faulty premise about available relief: even without LHEPA, petitioner could not obtain the compensatory emotional-distress damages he seeks under Title III of the ADA or under § 504 in this kind of private enforcement action. Respondents also defend the Louisiana courts’ use of LHEPA as a permissible state-law limitation applicable during the declared emergency, and contend petitioner’s preemption assertions were conclusory and unsupported. In their framing, because the petition either seeks remedies federal law does not allow or fails to plausibly plead the heightened culpability required during the emergency, certiorari is unwarranted.
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. 212 (2022) (limits emotional distress damages under Spending Clause statutes such as § 504)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023) (state COVID immunity interpretation; cited as comparative authority in briefing)
Resurgens, LLC v. Ervin, 894 S.E.2d 408 (Ga. 2023) (state COVID immunity interpretation; cited as comparative authority in briefing)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right that Felder and Howlett generally prohibit a State from superimposing a special heightened-fault immunity as a substantive defense to a federal claim in state court, and I accept that principle. But Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh persuasively identify a threshold vehicle problem: on this record, given Title III’s primarily prospective remedy and Cummings’ limits on § 504 emotional-distress damages, it is not clear that LHEPA actually foreclosed any federally authorized relief as applied here rather than duplicating federal remedial limits. Justice Sotomayor’s point that Supremacy Clause conflicts can exist without a damages showing is important, yet our institutional practice of deciding constitutional conflicts narrowly counsels against announcing a broad preemption rule where the alleged conflict may not be outcome-determinative on the pleadings. Consistent with minimalism, I would affirm (or consider DIG) and await a cleaner case where a plaintiff plausibly seeks federal relief that the state overlay concretely blocks.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedies objection assumes preemption requires a showing that LHEPA is outcome-determinative on this plaintiff’s damages theories, but Felder and Howlett treat the constitutional conflict as the State’s displacement of the federal rule of decision by interposing a special substantive immunity or heightened fault element against a federal claim. Even if Title III is largely injunctive and Cummings narrows § 504 damages, those are federal remedial limits; they do not authorize Louisiana to condition the existence of federal liability (or the availability of federally authorized prospective relief) on gross negligence or willful misconduct. Justice Alito’s framing of LHEPA as merely regulating “civil liability” during emergencies fails textually as applied here because it operates as an added substantive defense to federal rights, which the Supremacy Clause—under its original meaning and our cases—does not permit. The proper narrowness is to hold LHEPA preempted as applied to the federal causes of action and then let federal remedial doctrine determine what relief, if any, remains.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right to press Felder and Howlett: a State generally may not interpose a special substantive immunity or heightened-fault overlay to alter the federal rule of decision in its courts. But I remain persuaded by the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle point that, on these pleadings and given Title III’s largely injunctive private remedy plus Cummings’ contraction of § 504 damages, it is not shown that LHEPA, as applied here, concretely nullified any federally authorized relief rather than merely foreclosing damages theories federal law already withholds. Justice Sotomayor’s contention that preemption does not require damages foreclosure is forceful as a general proposition, yet in this emergency-management setting I would avoid announcing a broad as-applied preemption rule without a clearer, outcome-determinative conflict—especially where the practical availability of prospective relief under federal law is not developed. If a future case squarely shows LHEPA blocking an otherwise-available federal injunction or cognizable compensatory damages, Felder/Howlett would likely control; this record does not.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedy concern is the strongest point for the Respondent, but it misconceives the nature of the Supremacy Clause conflict identified in Felder and Howlett: the constitutional injury occurs when a State alters the federal rule of decision by adding a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct overlay, not only when we can already quantify a foreclosed damages award on this record. Even accepting Title III’s generally injunctive-only private remedy and Cummings’s contraction of § 504 emotional-distress damages, LHEPA still predictably obstructs federally authorized prospective relief by raising the liability threshold at the pleading stage, when disabled patients need timely access to court. Justice Alito’s framing of LHEPA as merely regulating “civil liability” during emergencies fails as applied here because the statute is being used as a substantive defense to federal discrimination claims, effectively rewriting federal elements and defenses rather than neutrally channeling state tort exposure. The narrower, institutionally cautious path is not affirmance, but an as-applied holding that LHEPA cannot govern the liability standard for the federal claims, leaving federal remedial limits to do their own work.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedies point is the strongest counter: if federal law already limits damages (Cummings) and Title III is largely injunctive, we should be cautious about deciding a broad preemption question on a thin record. But Felder and Howlett treat the constitutional injury as the State’s displacement of the federal rule of decision in its courts by interposing a special immunity/heightened-fault overlay—not as a showing that the plaintiff ultimately would win money damages on these pleadings. Even on a pragmatic view, LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct requirement functions as a substantive defense that can block federally authorized prospective relief (and any federal compensatory damages that remain) at the threshold, creating an obstacle to Congress’s enforcement scheme; the narrower, workable path is to hold LHEPA preempted as applied to the federal claims while leaving Louisiana free to apply it to state-law causes and to let federal remedial limits do their own work. Justice Alito’s characterization of LHEPA as a neutral emergency “civil liability” limit doesn’t fit this application because it is being used to reengineer liability elements for federal discrimination claims, which Felder/Howlett forbid.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedy concern does not defeat preemption because it mislocates the Supremacy Clause injury: under Felder and Howlett, the constitutional problem is Louisiana’s attempt to supply a state-law substantive defense (gross negligence/willful misconduct) that alters the federal rule of decision, not whether this particular plaintiff can ultimately recover a specific category of damages after Cummings. Even if Title III is largely injunctive and § 504 damages are narrowed, those are federal remedial choices; they do not authorize a State to condition federal liability or the availability of prospective relief on a state emergency immunity. Justice Alito’s framing of LHEPA as merely regulating “civil liability” during emergencies fails as applied here because it operates as an added fault element to federal discrimination claims—precisely what Felder/Howlett prohibit in state courts adjudicating federal rights. The narrow course is to hold LHEPA preempted as applied to the federal causes of action, leaving remedial limits to federal law and LHEPA’s operation to state-law claims.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are right on the core merits principle: under Felder and Howlett, a State generally may not apply a special heightened-fault “immunity” that functions as a substantive defense to a federal cause of action in its own courts. But Chief Justice Roberts’s vehicle concern still controls for me as an institutional matter: on this record, given Title III’s largely prospective remedy and Cummings’s constraints on § 504 emotional-distress damages, it is not sufficiently clear that LHEPA, as applied here, actually forecloses any federally authorized relief in a concrete, outcome-determinative way rather than addressing remedies federal law already limits. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch respond that preemption can exist absent damages foreclosure, and that is true in the abstract, but I would avoid announcing a broad Supremacy Clause rule about state emergency-liability regimes where the asserted conflict may be largely theoretical in this posture. I would affirm (or dispose narrowly) and leave Felder/Howlett’s application to a cleaner case where a plaintiff plausibly seeks specific federal relief that the state overlay demonstrably blocks.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest objection—vehicle/remedy—arguing the record does not show LHEPA foreclosed any federally authorized relief given Title III’s largely injunctive remedy and Cummings’ limits on § 504 damages. But under Felder and Howlett, the Supremacy Clause problem is the State’s interposition of a heightened-fault “immunity” that operates as a substantive defense altering the federal rule of decision in state court; that conflict does not turn on whether a particular damages theory ultimately survives federal remedial doctrine. Even if Cummings independently narrows damages, Louisiana still cannot condition federal liability or access to federally authorized prospective relief on a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct overlay Congress did not enact—federal elements and defenses govern, and federal remedial limits can do their own work afterward. Justice Alito’s framing of LHEPA as a general emergency “civil liability” measure does not avoid preemption when, as applied to ADA/§ 504 claims, it functions precisely as the kind of substantive immunity Felder/Howlett forbid.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedies concern is the strongest pushback, but it treats preemption as turning on whether this plaintiff can ultimately recover a particular category of damages on this record. Under Felder and Howlett—as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize—the Supremacy Clause problem arises when a State interposes a heightened-fault immunity that functions as a substantive defense and thereby alters the federal rule of decision for ADA/§ 504 claims in state court, including by impeding timely prospective relief. Justice Alito’s characterization of LHEPA as a neutral emergency “civil liability” limit does not answer that, as applied here, the statute redefines the federal duty by conditioning liability on gross negligence/willful misconduct rather than the federal nondiscrimination standard. A pragmatist approach still favors narrowness: reverse on preemption as applied to federal causes of action and leave federal remedial limits (including Cummings) to control the available relief without letting a State rewrite the threshold elements.

John Roberts.reasoning: Even assuming a serious Supremacy Clause question when a state “immunity” or heightened fault rule is applied to a federally created cause of action in state court, this petition is a poor vehicle because the relief sought appears largely unavailable under governing federal law: Title III of the ADA generally affords injunctive relief rather than damages, and under § 504 (a Spending Clause statute) this Court has held emotional-distress damages are not recoverable. See Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. 212 (2022). Given those remedial limits, the Louisiana courts’ reliance on LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard does not cleanly present a case where a state rule demonstrably “alters the outcome” of a viable federal damages claim, and deciding the broad preemption issue here risks an unnecessarily sweeping ruling. Consistent with judicial minimalism and preserving institutional legitimacy, I would not disturb the judgment on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not permit Louisiana to alter the elements of federally created causes of action under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by importing a state-law gross-negligence/willful-misconduct requirement as a categorical bar to liability. Under Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), state-law immunities or special defenses that would “thwart the congressional remedy” for a federal civil-rights claim are preempted when applied in state court to federal claims. Whatever limitations exist on remedies—e.g., Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. 212 (2022), on emotional-distress damages under Spending Clause statutes—do not authorize a State to rewrite the substantive standard of federal nondiscrimination duties. Because LHEPA’s heightened fault standard would make federal disability-rights protections contingent on a State emergency immunity regime, it conflicts with the federal statutory scheme and must give way.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause forbids a State from rewriting federal causes of action, see Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), but this record suggests the Louisiana courts’ invocation of LHEPA functions chiefly as a limitation on state-law “civil liability” during a declared emergency rather than a categorical bar to federal injunctive relief. Practically, petitioner’s theory depends heavily on damages remedies that federal law largely withholds here: Title III of the ADA generally provides injunctive relief, not compensatory damages, and Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. 212 (2022), forecloses emotional-distress damages under § 504 (a Spending Clause statute). Given those remedial limits, applying LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold does not clearly “thwart the congressional remedy” in the way Felder condemned, and I would not use this case—on these pleadings and remedies—to announce a broad preemption rule that would expose emergency healthcare decisions to expansive liability. The safer, more textually grounded course is to deny petitioner’s requested displacement and affirm the state court’s application of the emergency-liability standard in this context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, Louisiana may not apply LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct immunity to alter the elements or effectively bar federally created disability-discrimination claims under ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504, because state law cannot condition or frustrate federal rights in state courts. As in Felder v. Casey and Haywood v. Drown, a state rule—whether styled as immunity or a heightened fault requirement—that uniquely burdens federal civil-rights enforcement stands as an obstacle to Congress’s remedial scheme and undermines nationwide uniformity. Respondents’ remedial argument does not cure the displacement problem: even if Cummings limits emotional-distress damages under § 504 and Title III generally provides only injunctive relief, plaintiffs remain entitled to pursue the federal causes of action and available remedies without being converted into state tort claims by a state emergency statute. Allowing crisis-era immunities to swallow federal antidiscrimination duties would disproportionately harm vulnerable patients denied medically necessary care and would weaken access to justice precisely when it matters most.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Louisiana’s LHEPA gross-negligence/willful-misconduct immunity cannot be applied to re-engineer the elements of federally created disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12181–12189, and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. § 794, because state law may not condition or narrow federal rights and liabilities in state-court adjudication under the Supremacy Clause. Under Felder v. Casey and Howlett v. Rose, a state court must entertain federal causes of action on federally prescribed terms and cannot interpose state-law immunities or heightened standards that function as an obstacle to Congress’s enforcement scheme. Even if respondents are correct that Cummings limits certain damages under § 504, that remedial constraint is a federal-law question that does not license a state to add a gross-negligence element to liability or bar otherwise-available federal relief (e.g., injunctive relief under Title III). The better reading preserves statutory coherence and workability: state emergency-immunity rules may govern state tort claims, but they cannot displace federal civil-rights standards when the plaintiff pleads a federal ADA/RA violation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law immunity or heightened culpability requirement in a way that effectively narrows or defeats a federally created cause of action. This Court’s decisions in Felder v. Casey and Howlett v. Rose make clear that state rules—however framed—are preempted when they impose special burdens or defenses that alter the elements or enforcement of federal rights in state court. LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold, as applied to ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 discrimination claims, functions not as a neutral procedural rule but as a substantive redefinition of federal liability, and thus cannot displace Congress’s chosen standards. Whatever limits exist on remedies under federal law (e.g., Cummings limiting certain damages under § 504), those remedial constraints do not authorize a State to rewrite the federal claim’s elements via an emergency immunity statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Even assuming (under Haywood v. Drown and related Supremacy Clause cases) that a state may not apply an immunity rule that effectively nullifies a federally created cause of action in state court, this petition is a poor vehicle because the remedies sought appear largely unavailable as a matter of federal law. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, § 504 (a Spending Clause statute) does not permit recovery of emotional-distress damages, and Title III of the ADA generally authorizes only prospective injunctive relief in private suits, which substantially undercuts petitioner’s claim of prejudicial state-law displacement. Given those federal remedial limits and the absence of a clean, outcome-determinative conflict showing that LHEPA changed the availability of federally authorized relief, I would deny relief and vote for the respondents.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law immunity that “is not available to the defendant in a similar suit brought in a federal court” to defeat or rewrite the elements of a federally created cause of action. Howlett v. Rose holds that state courts must entertain federal claims on the same substantive terms as federal law provides, and may not interpose state-law defenses that function as substantive immunities inconsistent with federal rights. LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct requirement, as applied here to ADA Title III and § 504 claims, operates not as a neutral procedural rule but as a heightened substantive fault element that narrows federal liability beyond the statutes’ text and federally recognized standards. While Cummings limits certain damages under § 504, that remedial constraint does not authorize States to add an across-the-board immunity that bars or dilutes federal discrimination claims themselves during an emergency.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Louisiana may not, consistent with the Supremacy Clause, apply LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct immunity to effectively rewrite the elements of federal disability-discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act; doing so risks nullifying federally created rights and undermining uniform enforcement in state courts. Under Felder v. Casey, a state rule that immunizes or conditions liability in a way that “thwart[s] the congressional remedy” is preempted when applied to federal civil-rights claims, and LHEPA’s heightened-fault overlay functions as precisely that kind of obstacle. Respondents are right that remedies are limited (e.g., Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller bars emotional-distress damages under § 504), but limited remedies do not authorize a State to impose additional substantive hurdles that could foreclose even available federal relief (including injunctive relief under Title III and appropriate relief under § 504). Given the procedural-fairness and practical-consequences concerns, federal antidiscrimination standards—not emergency-era state immunity—must govern the elements of these federal causes of action in state court.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a state public-health-emergency immunity statute (Louisiana’s LHEPA) may be applied in state court to heighten or extinguish liability for federal disability-discrimination causes of action under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Health Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA) immunity provisions (granting civil liability immunity to healthcare providers during a declared public health emergency except for gross negligence or willful misconduct), as applied to federal claims under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that Louisiana courts improperly treated his ADA and Rehabilitation Act discrimination suit like a state tort claim by importing LHEPA’s heightened fault standard (gross negligence/willful misconduct) into federal civil-rights causes of action; he contends this state-law immunity regime conflicts with and is preempted by federal law because it alters the elements and enforceability of federally created rights, making federal disability protections conditional during emergencies and undermining national uniformity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue certiorari should be denied because petitioner’s damages theory is legally unavailable regardless of LHEPA (emotional distress/compensatory damages are not recoverable under Title III and are limited under § 504, citing federal precedent), and because Louisiana’s application of LHEPA as a civil-liability immunity during the COVID-era does not present a cert-worthy federal question (including that petitioner’s preemption assertions were conclusory and that the state courts’ dismissal can be affirmed on remedial grounds independent of the immunity issue).
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. ___ (2022)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605 (Conn. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest merits point: under Felder and Howlett/Haywood, a State generally may not superadd an “immunity” or heightened-fault rule that effectively rewrites the substantive standards of a federal cause of action in state court. But Justice Alito’s vehicle concern remains dispositive for me as a minimalist matter: if Title III is principally injunctive and Cummings substantially forecloses the compensatory-damages theory driving the § 504 claim, it is not clear on this record that LHEPA is outcome-determinative as to any federally available relief, which is the predicate that gives Felder/Haywood their bite here. I would avoid a broad Supremacy Clause holding about state emergency regimes where independent federal remedial limits likely resolve the case, leaving a cleaner preemption question for a future case in which a viable federal remedy is clearly extinguished solely by the state statute. Thomas and Gorsuch are right that States cannot rewrite federal law, but I do not think we should reach that constitutional question without first establishing that the alleged state-law conflict matters to the relief federal law actually authorizes in this suit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s vehicle/remedy objection does not cure the error actually embodied in the state-court judgment: Louisiana applied LHEPA to superadd a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct requirement to federal ADA/§ 504 claims, which conflicts with the Supremacy Clause’s command that valid federal law be applied as written. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize via Howlett and Haywood (and Felder), a State may not interpose a state-law immunity or heightened-fault overlay that functionally alters the elements/defenses of a federally created right in state court. Even if Cummings and Title III ultimately limit what remedies are available, those are federal constraints to be applied on remand; they do not authorize a State to rewrite Congress’s chosen liability standard. Because the dismissal rested on LHEPA as a dispositive defense to federal claims, I would reverse to correct that nonuniform, state-imposed alteration of federal law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest merits point from Howlett/Haywood/Felder: a State cannot re-label a substantive rewrite of a federal cause of action as “immunity” and thereby alter federal liability standards. But Chief Justice Roberts’ vehicle/remedy objection remains decisive for me: if, on this record, Title III is principally injunctive and Cummings likely forecloses the compensatory-damages theory under § 504, it is not clear that LHEPA is actually extinguishing any federally available relief in a way that is outcome-determinative, which is what gave Felder and Haywood practical bite. Under a restrained approach mindful of the significant real-world consequences for state emergency-response regimes, I would not announce a broad Supremacy Clause rule without a clean showing that a viable federal remedy is being nullified solely by LHEPA; any limits on relief should be resolved by federal remedial doctrine first.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedy point has force as a restraint instinct, but it does not justify affirming a judgment that rests on an impermissible state-law rewrite of federal liability. Even if Title III ultimately yields only injunctive relief and Cummings narrows § 504 damages, those are federal constraints to be applied on remand; they do not authorize Louisiana to interpose LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold as a substantive defense that changes the elements of ADA/§ 504 enforcement in state court, which Howlett, Haywood, and Felder forbid—as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress. Justice Jackson is right to worry about deciding more than necessary, so our rule can be narrow: States may apply neutral procedures, but they may not categorically immunize or heighten the fault standard for federal disability-rights claims based on state emergency policy. Because the state court’s LHEPA dismissal is itself the federal error, remedial uncertainty is not an off-ramp; it is an issue for the lower courts under federal law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedy off-ramp is the strongest counterargument: if Title III is essentially injunctive and Cummings sharply limits § 504 damages, we should avoid a broad constitutional holding. But as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Barrett stress, that framing doesn’t match the judgment below—Louisiana treated LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold as a substantive defense altering federal liability, which Howlett/Haywood/Felder forbid regardless of what federal remedies ultimately survive. Even if federal law later narrows relief, that is federal law doing the limiting; it does not authorize a State to rewrite the elements/defenses of the federal claim as a condition of adjudication in state court. I would reverse narrowly to correct that Supremacy Clause error and leave Title III/Cummings remedial questions for remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s vehicle/remedy point presses a genuine restraint concern, but it does not justify affirming a judgment that rests on a state-law rewrite of federal elements/defenses. As Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas stress via Howlett and Haywood (and Felder), the Supremacy Clause forbids Louisiana from superadding LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to ADA/§ 504 liability, regardless of whether federal law later narrows remedies under Title III or Cummings—those are federal limitations to be applied on remand, not a license for state alteration of the right. The “outcome-determinative” framing is misplaced here because the error below is structural: the state court dismissed by importing a state defense into federal claims, creating nonuniform enforcement of federal law in state courts. We can reverse narrowly—holding only that LHEPA cannot change the substantive standard for federal disability claims—while leaving remedial questions entirely to federal law on remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas, Justice Kagan, and Justice Gorsuch persuasively frame the state court’s move as a straightforward Howlett/Haywood problem—Louisiana cannot superadd a gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold to federal ADA/§ 504 liability and call it “immunity.” But I remain most persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s antecedent vehicle point: on this record, Title III’s remedial scheme is largely injunctive and Cummings significantly constrains compensatory damages under § 504, so it is not clear LHEPA is outcome-determinative as to any federally available remedy here. Under a minimalist, institutionally cautious approach, I would avoid a broad Supremacy Clause ruling with uncertain spillover for state emergency-response regimes when independent federal remedial limits may resolve (or at least substantially narrow) the case. If the petitioner can identify a concrete, federally available form of relief that LHEPA alone extinguishes, then Howlett/Haywood would likely control in a future, cleaner vehicle.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s vehicle argument—that Title III and Cummings may independently curtail the damages theory here—has real force as a restraint principle, but it does not confront the state court’s actual ground of decision: importing LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold as a categorical defense to federal ADA/§ 504 liability. Under Howlett and Haywood (as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize), a State may apply neutral procedures but may not alter the elements or defenses of a federal cause of action in its own courts, even if federal law ultimately limits remedies. Because any remedial narrowing must come from federal text and precedent (including Cummings) rather than state emergency policy, I would reverse on the Supremacy Clause point and leave the precise scope of federal relief to be sorted on remand under federal law. I do not see a sufficiently clear, record-grounded alternative disposition on Title III/Cummings that would justify affirming a judgment that rests on an impermissible state-law rewrite of federal standards.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s point most directly answers my restraint concern: whatever Title III and Cummings ultimately do to remedies, the judgment below turned on importing LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct threshold as a dispositive defense to federal ADA/§ 504 liability, which Howlett/Haywood/Felder treat as an impermissible state-law rewrite of federal rights. The Chief Justice’s vehicle argument is strongest—if federal law already forecloses the relief sought, we should avoid unnecessary constitutional rulings—but here that is not clear enough to affirm, because even injunctive relief (and potentially other forward-looking remedies) may remain and would still be affected by a categorical state “immunity” overlay. Under a pragmatic approach focused on procedural fairness and the practical consequence of uniform federal enforcement, I would reverse narrowly: Louisiana may apply neutral procedures, but it cannot use LHEPA to alter the substantive standard of liability/defenses for federal disability claims, leaving federal remedial limits to be applied on remand. That path corrects the specific Supremacy Clause error without announcing a broad rule about all emergency regimes.

John Roberts.reasoning: I would vote to affirm on the narrower, antecedent ground that petitioner’s remedial theory is unavailable under the relevant federal statutes, avoiding a broad preemption ruling with uncertain downstream effects on state emergency frameworks. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, emotional-distress damages are not recoverable under Spending Clause statutes like § 504, and Title III of the ADA generally authorizes only injunctive relief, making it doubtful that petitioner can obtain the compensatory relief he seeks regardless of Louisiana’s LHEPA immunity overlay. Given that disposition, the Court need not decide whether applying LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard to ADA/§ 504 claims creates an obstacle to Congress’s purposes under the Supremacy Clause. Deciding no more than necessary best preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves for another day a case squarely presenting a live conflict like Haywood v. Drown where state law functionally nullifies a federal cause of action in state court.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply a state-law immunity regime to alter the substantive liability standard Congress created for federal civil-rights actions, whether by adding a gross-negligence element or by extinguishing liability during an emergency. This Court has held that state rules singling out federal causes of action for special burdens or immunities are preempted and must give way to the federal right as written, even when the claim is litigated in state court. See Haywood v. Drown, 556 U.S. 729 (2009), and Howlett v. Rose, 496 U.S. 356 (1990). Louisiana’s LHEPA may govern state tort claims, but it cannot condition or narrow federally conferred rights under Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by imposing defenses Congress did not enact.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Even assuming a serious Supremacy Clause question could arise if a State used an emergency-immunity statute to negate a federal cause of action, this case is a poor vehicle because petitioner’s damages theory appears independently foreclosed under federal law. Title III of the ADA principally authorizes injunctive relief, and under § 504 this Court in Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller held that emotional-distress damages are not recoverable, substantially limiting what petitioner can obtain regardless of LHEPA’s gross-negligence standard. Where the federal remedial scheme already restricts liability, it is unnecessary to decide whether Louisiana’s LHEPA creates an “obstacle” to federal rights in the manner condemned in Haywood v. Drown, and state courts may dismiss on those independent federal grounds. Given the practical consequences during declared emergencies and the lack of a clean, dispositive conflict, I would deny relief and vote for respondents.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Louisiana’s LHEPA cannot be applied to federal ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 claims to impose a heightened gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard or confer categorical immunity, because that state-law regime would alter the enforceability and elements of federally created civil-rights claims and thus stands as an obstacle to Congress’s objectives under the Supremacy Clause. Under Felder v. Casey, state courts may apply their ordinary procedures to federal causes of action only so long as they do not impose outcome-determinative burdens that predictably defeat federal rights; importing LHEPA’s emergency immunity functions like the notice-of-claim barrier invalidated in Felder by making federal disability protections contingent on state emergency declarations. Respondents’ remedial arguments (including limits on damages under Cummings and Title III) go to what relief may be available, not to whether the State may rewrite federal liability standards; at most they support narrowing remedies, not extinguishing liability through state immunity. Because vulnerable disabled patients are most at risk during emergencies, allowing States to dilute federal disability protections at precisely that moment would undermine uniform national enforcement of the ADA and § 504.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Louisiana’s LHEPA immunity, as applied here, effectively rewrites the liability standard for federally created disability-discrimination causes of action by conditioning their enforceability on proof of gross negligence or willful misconduct, which conflicts with the remedial scheme Congress chose in Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. Under the Supremacy Clause and this Court’s reverse-Erie/obstacle-preemption line, state rules—whether styled as “immunity” or “heightened fault”—cannot nullify or substantially burden federal rights in state court, as in Felder v. Casey and Haywood v. Drown (and consistent with Williams v. Reed’s rejection of state-law immunization of § 1983 claims). Respondents’ remedial arguments (e.g., limits on damages under Cummings) may narrow what relief is available, but they do not authorize a State to import a different liability threshold that could extinguish federal claims altogether. A workable, coherent rule is that states may apply neutral state procedures, but may not apply emergency-immunity regimes that alter the elements or defenses of federal civil-rights actions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause does not permit a State to “condition” or effectively defeat a federally created civil-rights cause of action by importing a state-law immunity or heightened fault requirement that Congress did not enact. Under Felder v. Casey, state courts entertaining federal claims may not apply state-law notice/immunity rules that burden federal rights and remedies; Louisiana’s LHEPA, as used here to require gross negligence or willful misconduct for ADA Title III and Rehabilitation Act § 504 liability, alters the elements and enforceability of those federal causes of action. Whatever limits exist on remedies (e.g., Cummings limiting emotional-distress damages under Spending Clause statutes like § 504), those remedial constraints do not authorize a State to add extra defenses that narrow federal liability itself. Because LHEPA’s immunity regime stands as an obstacle to the full operation of federal disability-discrimination law as written, it must yield when applied to extinguish or heighten liability on these federal claims in state court.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Even assuming Felder v. Casey bars states from applying immunity rules that thwart federally created civil-rights remedies in state court, this case is a poor vehicle because petitioner’s requested relief appears largely unavailable under the federal statutes regardless of LHEPA. Title III of the ADA generally provides injunctive relief rather than compensatory damages, and under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller emotional-distress damages are not recoverable under Spending Clause statutes like § 504—making it hard to show that Louisiana’s LHEPA “civil liability” immunity meaningfully diminishes a federal remedy here. Given those remedial limits and the possibility of affirmance on independent federal-law grounds, I would deny the petition and vote to uphold the dismissal without reaching a broad preemption ruling about LHEPA’s interaction with ADA/§ 504. Judicial restraint and practical workability counsel against announcing a sweeping Supremacy Clause rule in a case where the federal damages theory likely fails anyway.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Supremacy Clause, a State may not apply its own immunity or heightened-fault regime in a way that substantively alters the elements or enforceability of a federally created cause of action, even when the claim is litigated in state court. Louisiana’s LHEPA (gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard) functions as a state-law defense that would narrow Title III of the ADA and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act beyond their text and Congress’s chosen enforcement scheme, creating nonuniform, emergency-contingent federal rights. This Court’s decisions in Howlett v. Rose and Felder v. Casey prohibit state rules that “condition” or “discriminate against” federal claims by imposing additional obstacles or defenses not found in federal law; LHEPA’s application here does exactly that by importing a heightened culpability element. Respondents’ remedial arguments (e.g., limits on damages under Cummings) may affect what relief is available, but they do not justify allowing a State to extinguish federal liability altogether through state immunity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Even assuming Louisiana courts erred by importing LHEPA’s gross-negligence/willful-misconduct standard into federal ADA Title III and § 504 claims, this case is a poor vehicle because petitioner’s requested damages appear independently unavailable under federal law. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, § 504 (a Spending Clause statute) does not allow recovery of emotional-distress damages, and Title III of the ADA generally authorizes only injunctive relief (not compensatory damages), so the asserted liability would likely fail regardless of any state-law immunity overlay. Given those remedial limits, the Supremacy Clause/Howlett-type question about state-law immunities altering federal rights may not be outcome-determinative here, making cert-worthy review unwarranted on this record. Procedural fairness and pragmatic consequences counsel against taking a case that could be resolved on federal remedial grounds without reaching the broader preemption issue.
